transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-26
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: available (link sent)
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Jon Park (Lead ML Eng, Sable), Maria Lopez (CTO, Sable), Ethan Chu (Eng Mgr, Sable)

Summary (auto):
- Deep dive on KV cache eviction patterns, paging, and strategies for long-context workloads.
- Discussed root causes (memory pressure from long sequences, prefix reuse fragmentation, cross-session cold start).
- Agreed next steps: share logs, run targeted benchmarks on Dedicated, test prefix pinning and quantized KV to reduce memory.

Topics: KV cache eviction; paging to SSD; long-context (10k-50k tokens); prefix reuse across sessions; batching tradeoffs; quantization reductions; VPC/private deployment constraints.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. quick intro, i'm alex from redwood, this is priya the se who knows the runtime inside out.
[00:08] Jon: thanks alex, we really wanna dig into the kv cache eviction stuff - we've been seeing p95 latency spikes and also some strange paging.
[00:14] Priya: cool, can you give a couple quick examples of what you see in prod? even a ballpark sequence length, or whether it's single long session or many shorter ones?
[00:22] Jon: yeah so we have chat sessions that accumulate, some users go to 20k-40k tokens, often with a lot of reused prefixes - like standard prompts for customer profiles - but the runtime seems to evict prefixes and then regen them frequently which spikes latency. we also saw paging events that show up right before 500-800ms delays.
[00:45] Maria: and to add, we tried increasing batch size but that made the issue worse in p95, so we rolled it back.
[00:52] Priya: okay makes sense. a few high-level causes: (1) per-GPU kv memory pressure from long KV stores, (2) prefix fragmentation where many similar prefixes aren't colocated in cache, and (3) paging when the cache implementation tries to spill to host or SSD.
[01:10] Ethan: when you say host, do you mean CPU memory or disk? we thought redwood cached on GPU only.
[01:16] Priya: good q - by default the runtime keeps KV on GPU memory. when GPU memory is insufficient we have eviction/paging strategies: we first evict least-recently-used (LRU) KV entries; if configured, we can page to CPU host RAM, or further to NVMe-backed storage. paging to CPU adds ~10-30ms typically, NVMe can add 100-500ms depending on IO. that matches the spikes you saw.
[01:40] Jon: the spikes we saw were near 300-700ms, so nvme paging seems likely. any quick wins to reduce that?
[01:47] Priya: yes. quick wins: increase per-GPU KV budget (if you have slack on Dedicated), enable intelligent prefix pinning for hot prefixes, and enable compressed/quantized KV storage which reduces KV footprint by ~2-4x depending on 8-bit/4-bit quantization.
[02:05] Alex: important note - quantized KV trades a small accuracy delta for memory saving. we can run a regression test on your prompt set to measure quality impact.
[02:13] Maria: how mature is the quantized kv path? are there gotchas for production?
[02:17] Priya: it's stable; we've rolled it out on several customers. gotchas: some model ops interplay with attention kernels means you need to pick matching quant profile for your model architecture and seq length. also longer sequences may need slightly different per-layer quant thresholds. we provide recommended profiles in the doc link - redwood.ai/docs/kv-quant-profiles (we'll send exact link).
[02:36] [00:00 - 02:36 elapsed]
[02:37] Jon: about prefix reuse - we observed that similar prefixes across different sessions are evicted because the cache keys differ by small tokens (user ids or timestamps) - is there a strategy to canonicalize keys?
[02:47] Priya: yes, prefix normalization or canonicalization is a big win. you can map variable tokens (user ids, timestamps) to placeholders before sending to the runtime, which allows the same KV entries to be reused across sessions. we also support an API to indicate prefix groups (meta tags) so the runtime will co-locate them in the same cache shards.
[03:05] Ethan: is that manual or automatic? sounds like app-level work.
[03:09] Priya: partially app-level - replacements are done by your app - but we can supply a small library to help with canonicalization and instrumentation. we can also try prefix grouping heuristics server-side but app-level control is more deterministic.
[03:21] Maria: any tradeoffs if we canonicalize? do we lose context specificity?
[03:25] Priya: you only canonicalize the parts you know are noise (user id tokens etc). keep the semantic tokens. it's a bit of engineering but high ROI for workloads with lots of prompt templates.
[03:34] [03:34 - 12:34] (edited skip for time)
[12:35] Jon: ok, paging config - what params control when we spill to CPU vs NVMe?
[12:40] Priya: two knobs: kv_memory_threshold (percentage of GPU mem where eviction/paging triggers), and spill_target (none, host, nvme). we default at 85% kv_memory_threshold and spill_target=host for most hosted customers. Dedicated customers often set kv_memory_threshold to 92-95% and spill_target=none to force evictions only.
[12:58] Alex: if you want no spike tail latency, it's best to avoid nvme paging in the p95 path altogether - that means either allocate larger GPUs for your Dedicated pool or enable quantized storage to reduce footprint.
[13:11] Ethan: curious about shard placement - is cache sharded by conversation, user, or token range? we have microservices that route sessions.
[13:18] Priya: it's sharded by model instance and then by hash of conversation id by default. hot-spotting can be a problem; we have elastic shard rebalancing and we can use consistent hashing with replication to reduce eviction storms. for customers with many small sessions we recommend pooling sessions across shards to even utilization.
[13:38] Maria: you mentioned eviction storms - what does that look like in logs?
[13:42] Priya: you'll see rapid sequences of 'evict' events with the same shard id followed by many 'miss' and 'regen' entries; p95 latency will spike, and you'll see sudden increase in host IO.
[13:54] Jon: we have those exact logs. i'll attach them.
[13:58] Priya: perfect, those will let us correlate which prefixes are being evicted and when - we can suggest pinning or raising kv budgets for those shards.
[14:08] Alex: another step is warmup. if you have known sequences for specific customers you can pre-warm the cache after deploy or before expected peaks. That reduces cold regen latency.
[14:18] Ethan: how expensive is warmup? does it consume tokens we pay for?
[14:21] Priya: warmups do consume inference tokens if you do full forward passes, so it's a tradeoff. we support a 'kv-only' warmup mode that reconstructs cache entries without full token billing in some Dedicated setups; we'll need to enable that for you.
[14:34] [14:34 - 25:00]
[25:01] Maria: let's talk batching. we tried larger batches to improve throughput but saw p95 regress. what's the sweet spot?
[25:08] Priya: it's workload-dependent. batching improves throughput but increases tail latency for interactive requests because you wait to fill batch windows. Our runtime supports adaptive batching where we set a small max latency window (e.g., 5-10ms) and smaller batch caps for high-priority interactive routes. We recommend per-route configs: e.g., chat routes use max_batch_latency=8ms, background generation uses 50-100ms.
[25:33] Jon: any impact on kv cache with larger batches?
[25:36] Priya: yes - larger batches increase concurrent KV access and can amplify pressure on certain shards. If many sessions in a batch reference the same prefix, that's good (reuse). If they're diverse, more memory and eviction risk. So batching and cache behavior should be tuned together.
[25:50] Alex: quick note on quantization again - quantized KV reduces footprint but also reduces memory bandwidth and can slightly reduce compute latency because less data moves across PCI-e. That helps p95 in practice.
[26:05] Ethan: what's the expected quality delta? customers worry about hallucinations rising after quantize.
[26:10] Priya: on our internal evals for typical Llama-2 and similar families, with 8-bit kv quant we saw <0.5% drop on Rouge/BLEU-like metrics and negligible human-noticeable differences on chat flows. 4-bit is more aggressive and needs regression testing. we'll run your eval set to be safe.
[26:32] [26:32 - 40:00]
[40:01] Jon: we run in a VPC and security is strict; if we move to Dedicated or Private, any KV changes with encryption or KMS?
[40:09] Alex: KV entries are treated like ephemeral model cache - we don't persist them to customer S3 by default. For Private deployments we support customer KMS for keys and disk encryption for nvme spill. For Dedicated we can enable host encryption. audit logs are available for cache evictions and spills.
[40:26] Maria: and compliance - SOC2/ISO? we need that for procurement.
[40:30] Alex: we'll attach the SOC2 summary and the VPC/on-prem checklist in the follow up.
[40:36] Priya: also a note: for Private air-gapped deployments, the paging layer will be local NVMe only - so I/O latency depends on the host setup; we'll help size NVMe for your expected p95 targets.
[40:49] Jon: good to know.
[40:52] [40:52 - 55:00]
[55:01] Ethan: ok, so concrete experiments you'd recommend we run next?
[55:05] Priya: 1) baseline run on your current hosted config capturing evict, miss, regen rates, p50/p95 latency, and IO metrics; 2) repeat with 8-bit kv quant enabled; 3) repeat with kv_memory_threshold increased (if Dedicated possible), or move to larger GPU type; 4) try prefix canonicalization for a small set of templates. we'll help set these up and analyze.
[55:30] Alex: we'll prepare a benchmark sheet template and a runbook; priya will also share the config knobs and the API for prefix grouping.
[55:40] Jon: sounds great, i'll get logs and sample sessions over.
[55:44] Maria: schedule the benchmark run with us for week of april 6th - we prefer a morning slot PST.
[55:50] Alex: copying that.
[55:53] Priya: one last note - if you see eviction storms again, please capture a 2-minute flame of the logs and heap stats and send it to our se inbox; that's the fastest way for us to triage.
[56:05] Jon: will do. thanks everyone.
[56:08] Alex: great meeting, recap in the follow up email with artifacts and next steps.
